content: Phototoxicity is a phenomenon observed in live cells where the illumination of a fluorescent molecule, known as a fluorophore, leads to the selective death of the cells expressing it. In fluorescence microscopy, while the exact mechanisms are not fully understood, it is evident that the primary cause of phototoxicity is the formation of oxygen radicals. These radicals are generated due to non-radiative energy transfer. Typically, during fluorescence, photons of a specific wavelength excite the electrons of the fluorophore to higher energy states. When these excited electrons return to a lower energy state, they emit photons with lower energy, resulting in the emission of light at a longer wavelength. This phenomenon is referred to as the Stokes shift. However, not all the energy is utilized for this radiative energy transfer. In some cases, energy is transferred to oxygen molecules, leading to the formation of oxygen radicals. These radicals are highly toxic to living cells and can sometimes kill cells within seconds. The extent of phototoxicity in live cells is highly dependent on the type of fluorescent molecule used. The discovery and characterization of fluorescent proteins, such as green fluorescent protein (GFP), have provided biologists with fluorochromes that exhibit significantly weaker phototoxic effects compared to smaller, chemically synthesized fluorescent molecules like FITC or rhodamine. Despite this advancement, it remains critical to minimize both the energy level of the excitation light and the duration of illumination to ensure the long-term survival of living cells during fluorescent imaging. In humans, a phototoxic substance is defined as a chemical compound that becomes toxic only when exposed to light. Examples include: Certain medications, such as tetracycline antibiotics and methyl aminolevulinate. Some cold-pressed essential oils, such as bergamot oil. Certain plant juices, such as those from parsley or hogweed. To assess phototoxicity, the 3T3 Neutral Red Uptake Phototoxicity Test (3T3 NRU PT) is commonly used. This in vitro toxicological assay evaluates the cytotoxic and phototoxic effects of a test substance on murine fibroblasts in the presence or absence of UVA light. The 3T3 NRU PT identifies phototoxic effects by comparing the cytotoxicity of a test substance after exposure to a non-cytotoxic dose of UVA/visible light with its cytotoxicity in the absence of light. Cytotoxicity is measured as a concentration-dependent reduction in the uptake of the vital dye, Neutral Red. This assay can detect substances that are phototoxic in vivo after systemic application and distribution to the skin, as well as compounds that act as phototoxicants following topical application to the skin. The reliability and relevance of the 3T3 NRU PT have been evaluated and shown to be predictive when compared to acute phototoxicity effects observed in vivo in both animals and humans. This assay is relatively new and has been adopted by regulatory agencies such as the OECD and FDA as an accepted method for assessing the phototoxic potential of test substances. Other testing methods for phototoxicity assessment are also available. These include in vitro toxicology models that utilize reconstituted tissues and novel photo-sensitization testing models. These methods are being developed and explored to determine how a compound may react when applied to the skin and irradiated with solar-simulated light.
